title: Safe Tool Use Workflow
summary: This intermediate module teaches a repeatable workflow for reviewing, authorizing, executing, and verifying AI-assisted external actions. After completing it, learners can identify unsafe action requests, stop before unintended effects occur, and verify whether an authorized action produced the expected result.
objectives: Define the intended outcome and permitted action boundary before an external action begins.
Inspect proposed inputs, scope, access, and effects before authorizing an action.
Apply a stop condition when an action is ambiguous, unexpectedly broad, or difficult to reverse.
Compare observed results with expected results and record enough information for later review.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous citation was the internal path content/modules/ai-foundations/safe-tool-use-workflow.json, attributed to an unregistered publisher and never verified. That entry did not provide a directly accessible HTTPS source.

The cited source has been changed to the official National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework page. This correction affects the module's source provenance, verification date, review schedule, and the framing that connects the workflow to lifecycle risk management. Material not dependent on the invalid citation remains unchanged.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can read a proposed action, identify its inputs and expected output, and recognize that an external action can affect data or another system. It does not assume experience with any named product or provider.

An external action is any operation that can create, read, change, send, or delete something outside the immediate conversation. The workflow in this module converts lifecycle risk management into a practical sequence: define, inspect, authorize, execute, verify, and record.

sections.title: Define the intended boundary
paragraphs: Begin by stating the intended outcome in concrete terms. Then identify what may be acted on, what must remain untouched, and what result should be visible if the action succeeds. A request such as changing one specified record has a narrower boundary than changing every related record.

Do not treat a plausible interpretation as authorization. If the target, scope, or intended result is ambiguous, stop and obtain clarification before proceeding. This is the first stop condition in the workflow.
sections.callout: Before acting, be able to answer three questions: What exact outcome is intended, what may be affected, and what must not be affected?

sections.title: Inspect before authorization
paragraphs: Review the proposed action before it runs. Check the target, inputs, scope, requested access, expected effects, and whether the action can be reversed. Look for hidden expansion, such as an operation aimed at more items than the stated outcome requires.

Grant only the access needed for the defined action. If the proposed access or scope is broader than necessary, reduce it or stop. If an action is difficult to reverse or could produce a significant effect, require explicit human approval before execution.

A preview is useful only when it is compared with the intended boundary. If the preview includes an unexpected target or additional action, do not execute it merely because the rest of the preview looks correct.

sections.title: Execute with stop conditions
paragraphs: Execute only the reviewed action within the authorized boundary. Do not silently add follow-up actions, broaden the target, or reinterpret an error as permission to try a more invasive operation.

Stop if the action presented for execution differs from the reviewed proposal, if new access is requested, if the target changes, or if an unexpected effect appears. Return to inspection and authorization rather than continuing from an invalid assumption.

sections.title: Verify and record the result
paragraphs: After execution, compare the observed result with the expected result defined at the start. A completion message alone does not establish that the intended outcome occurred or that no unintended effect occurred.

If the result differs from the expectation, stop further actions, preserve the available evidence, and seek review before attempting a correction. An immediate retry can compound the original problem.

Record the intended outcome, authorized scope, action taken, observed result, and any exception. This record supports later review and makes it possible to determine where the workflow departed from the approved boundary.

sections.title: Workflow recap
paragraphs: The complete sequence is define, inspect, authorize, execute, verify, and record. At every transition, stop when the target, scope, access, reversibility, or observed effect no longer matches what was reviewed.

After completing this module, you can do more than recognize that external actions carry risk. You can establish an action boundary, test a proposal against that boundary, withhold authorization when it does not match, and verify the result after execution.

questions.prompt: What should happen before a proposed external action is inspected or authorized?
choices: Define the intended outcome and permitted action boundary
Execute the action once to discover its effects
Grant broad access to avoid interruptions
questions.explanation: The module begins with defining the intended outcome, what may be affected, what must remain untouched, and what result is expected.

questions.prompt: A preview includes an additional target that is outside the stated outcome. What is the correct response?
choices: Execute because most of the preview is correct
Expand the intended outcome to match the preview
Stop and resolve the mismatch before execution
Execute and inspect the additional target afterward
questions.explanation: An unexpected target falls outside the authorized boundary. The workflow requires stopping and returning to inspection and authorization.

questions.prompt: How should a learner verify an executed action?
choices: Accept a completion message as sufficient evidence
Compare the observed result with the expected result defined before execution
Repeat the action to see whether the same message appears
Assume success when no error is displayed
questions.explanation: Verification requires comparing the observed result with the previously defined expectation. A completion message by itself is not sufficient.

questions.prompt: What source-related correction does this update make?
choices: It replaces an unverified internal-path citation with an official HTTPS source
It adds a named provider's product documentation
It removes all source and review metadata
It replaces the workflow with a product-specific procedure
questions.explanation: The update replaces the never-verified internal-path citation with the official National Institute of Standards and Technology framework page and updates the associated verification metadata.
